title: Hacer, decir, poner, dar
topic: present tense of hacer, decir, poner, dar and their expressions
why: After ir, venir and salir, here are four verbs with an irregular first person (hago, digo, pongo, doy) used in loads of expressions. The lesson also teaches you to talk about the weather with hace and to split household chores, still in the present.

Hago, digo, pongo, doy

These four verbs have one thing in common: it's mostly the first person that's irregular. Once you've got hago, pongo and doy down, the rest is conjugated like a regular verb.

hacer (to do, to make)decir (to say)poner (to put)dar (to give)
yohagodigopongodoy
túhacesdicesponesdas
él, ella, ustedhacediceponeda
nosotros, nosotrashacemosdecimosponemosdamos
vosotros, vosotrashacéisdecísponéisdais
ellos, ellas, ustedeshacendicenponendan

What to notice

  • Hacer and poner: only the yo form changes (hago, pongo). Everything else is regular -er.
  • Decir is doubly irregular: digo with a g, and the e becomes i everywhere except with nosotros and vosotros (dices, dice, dicen but decimos, decís).
  • Dar gives doy, like soy, estoy and voy. Dais has no accent: it's one syllable, like vais.

The -go family

Make a list: tengo, vengo, salgo, hago, pongo, digo. Six very common verbs whose yo form ends in -go. If you're unsure about the first person of a common verb, think of this family.

The classic trap: \"hazo\" or \"haco\" for \"I do\". The only form is hago.

¿Qué haces los domingos? Hago deporte y doy un paseo.What do you do on Sundays? I play sports and go for a walk.
", "

The weather: hace calor

English says \"it's hot\"; Spanish says \"it makes heat\", with hace. And there's no subject, no \"it\": \"it's hot\" is simply hace calor.

SpanishEnglish
¿Qué tiempo hace?What's the weather like?
Hace calor. / Hace frío.It's hot. / It's cold.
Hace sol.It's sunny.
Hace viento.It's windy.
Hace buen tiempo. / Hace mal tiempo.The weather is nice. / The weather is bad.
Llueve. / Nieva.It's raining. / It's snowing.
Está nublado.It's cloudy.

Mucho, not muy

Calor, frío, sol and viento are nouns (el calor, el frío: \"heat\", \"cold\"). Remember the rule: muy goes before an adjective, mucho before a noun. So \"it's very hot\" is Hace mucho calor (\"it makes a lot of heat\"), never \"hace muy calor\".

Hace calor or tengo calor?

Hace calor is about the weather. For a person, Spanish uses tener, as for age: Tengo calor (I'm hot), ¿Tienes frío? (are you cold?). Literally: \"I have heat\", \"do you have cold?\".

Llueve and nieva come from llover and nevar: learn them as set forms, since you always talk about the weather in the 3rd person.

En Sevilla, en agosto, hace mucho calor.In Seville, in August, it's very hot.
", "

At home: the expressions

These verbs are used in set expressions. Some match English, others don't: that's where you need to be careful.

SpanishEnglishNote
hacer la comprato do the grocery shoppinglike \"do\"
hacer la comidato make lunch, to cooklike \"make\"
hacer la camato make the bedsame as English
hacer deporteto play sports, to exerciseno article
hacer los deberesto do homeworkwith the article
poner la mesato set the tableliterally \"put\" the table
poner la teleto turn on the TVliterally \"put on\" the TV
poner la lavadorato do a load of laundryliterally \"put on\" the washing machine
dar un paseoto go for a walkwith dar (\"give\"), not hacer
dar las graciasto say thank you, to thankwith dar

Decir

Decir is used like \"to say\" or \"to tell\": Digo la verdad (I tell the truth), Elena dice que no (Elena says no). When you haven't understood, ask ¿Qué dices? (what are you saying?).

One Spanish verb for two English ones: hacer means both \"do\" and \"make\". \"Make the bed\" and \"do sports\" both use it, as in hacer deporte.

Yo hago la comida y tú pones la mesa, ¿vale?I'll make lunch and you set the table, OK?
